title: Read and write numbers to 10 000 in standard, expanded and word form

lesson.title: Numbers to 10 000: Three Ways to Say the Same Number

steps.say: You already know that in a number like three hundred forty-seven, each digit has its own place. Today we take that same idea a little bigger, all the way up to ten thousand, and we learn that one number can be written in three different ways that all mean exactly the same thing.

Let's use a real number. Imagine a hockey arena in Vancouver with four thousand two hundred sixty-three seats. We write it like this: four, two, six, three. Look at where each digit sits. The four is in the thousands place, so it really means four thousand. The two sits in the hundreds place, so it means two hundred. The six is in the tens place, so it means sixty. And the three is in the ones place, so it just means three.

Here is the big idea. A digit's value comes from where it sits, not just from what it looks like. So when we stretch the number out and show each piece, we get four thousand plus two hundred plus sixty plus three. That is called expanded form. And when we say it out loud in words, it is four thousand two hundred sixty-three. Standard form, expanded form, word form. Three outfits, same number underneath.

visual.caption: The four pieces of 4263 lined up by size

steps.say: Now let's watch a mistake I see a lot. Some kids look at the number two thousand fifty and write it as two thousand plus five plus zero, because they see a five and a zero. But look where that five is sitting. It is in the tens place, so it is worth fifty, not five. And the zero in the hundreds place is doing an important job. It is holding the hundreds spot empty so the five stays in the tens. So the correct expanded form is two thousand plus fifty, and in words it is two thousand fifty.

visual.caption: 2050: the 0 holds the hundreds place open

steps.say: Let's finish with a small one so you can see the pieces with blocks. Three hundred twenty-four is three hundreds, two tens, and four ones. Count the blocks: three big flats, two rods, four little cubes. Three hundred plus twenty plus four. Same number, just wearing a different outfit.
So remember: a digit's value depends on the place it sits in, and standard form, expanded form, and word form are just three ways of saying that very same number.

lesson.answer: Where a digit sits tells you what it is worth — standard, expanded, and word form all say the same number.

practice.question: A school in Kelowna raised five thousand seven hundred eight dollars for a new playground. Write that amount in standard form using digits, and then write it in expanded form as a sum.
practice.answer: Standard form: 5708. Expanded form: 5000 + 700 + 8. (There are no tens, so the zero in the tens place holds that spot open — the 8 stays in the ones place.)
